part1: When studying history in school,
we often get the comforting feeling that it is a seamless, linear narrative:
one dynasty neatly follows another,
one empire replaces the next,
with every event stamped with clear dates,
prominent names, and tidy explanations.
Yet the truth is profoundly different.
The history we know is like a vast jigsaw puzzle missing most of its pieces.
There are centuries-long chasms of time from which virtually no written records survive.
There are civilizations that engineered underground urban drainage systems
a thousand years before Europeans achieved anything comparable,
yet we do not know what language they spoke,
which gods they worshipped, or why they walked away.
There are maritime kingdoms that once traded directly with the Roman Empire,
only to be buried so deeply that local descendants eventually forgot their very name.
In this video, we will journey across four such historical voids,
spanning four continents across nearly four thousand years.
The first void is the simultaneous, systemic collapse of
the entire eastern Mediterranean over three thousand years ago,
when multiple imperial superpowers vanished within decades,
and literacy was extinguished in many lands for centuries.
The second void is a South Asian civilization that left thousands of inscribed seals,
yet to this very day, no scholar has deciphered a single sentence.
The third void is a colossal prehistoric metropolis in the American heartland,
more populous than many contemporary European capitals,
suddenly abandoned without leaving a single written word of explanation.
And the fourth void, closest to home for us:
a wealthy maritime kingdom that once flourished right in the modern Mekong Delta,
which the world almost entirely forgot until
French archaeologists detected its canal networks from aerial reconnaissance photographs,
initiating excavations in 1942.
What unites all four of these enigmas?
Not sensationalized 'supernatural mysteries' or 'lost alien technology' as clickbait often claims,
but rigorous, profound scientific questions
that archaeologists are piecing together shard by shard,
sediment core by core, genome by genome.
Let us begin.
part2: Imagine our world around the year 1250 BC.
This was an era historians designate as the Late Bronze Age,
resembling a miniature, interconnected globalized world.
Pharaonic Egypt prospered along the fertile banks of the Nile.
The mighty Hittite Empire dominated Anatolia, modern-day Turkey.
The wealthy Mycenaean citadels of Greece gleamed with gold.
Bustling merchant port cities lined the Levant.
Babylon commanded the Mesopotamian floodplains.
All were interwoven through an intricate web of international trade:
tin imported from distant Afghan mountains, copper mined in Cyprus,
luxury treasures circulating across the Mediterranean.
Monarchs exchanged diplomatic correspondence, royal brides, and commercial fleets.
Then, between roughly 1200 and 1150 BC, almost all of it collapsed in ruin.
The Mycenaean palace centers in Greece—Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos—were torched or abandoned.
The Hittite Empire vanished entirely from the geopolitical map.
Flourishing harbor cities across Cyprus, Syria, and the Levant were reduced to ash.
Egypt survived, but barely,
depleted of treasury and military reserves,
marking what historians consider the start of its irreversible long-term decline.
What was particularly terrifying was not merely the war, but that literacy vanished.
Complex administrative writing systems dissolved along with the palaces that maintained them.
In Greece, writing ceased for hundreds of years,
plunging the region into what historians term the Greek Dark Ages—
frequently regarded as the very first 'dark age' in world history.
There is a haunting archaeological detail from this collapse:
at several excavated sites, archaeologists uncovered clay tablets still resting inside kilns,
baked by the very fires that incinerated the palaces, never retrieved by their scribes—
testament to an organized society cut down in the middle of a working day.
So what truly caused this apocalypse?
The prime historical suspect was long identified as a mysterious confederation
that Egyptian hieroglyphs called the 'Peoples of the Sea', or the Sea Peoples.
These were seaborne marauders arriving from the islands,
assaulting the Nile Delta,
dramatically depicted on temple reliefs commissioned by Pharaoh Ramesses the Third.
Ramesses III defeated them, but scholars emphasize
that the exhausting defense bankrupted the royal treasury.
Yet there is a striking historiographical truth: the term 'Sea Peoples' never appears in ancient texts.
It was coined by French Egyptologist Gaston Maspero in 1881.
Egyptian scribes merely described disparate groups arriving 'from the sea' or 'from the islands',
offering sparse details to establish their precise origins.
Contemporary archaeologists increasingly view them not as a unified invading army,
but as an eclectic mosaic of displaced peoples,
speaking multiple languages,
likely including early Mycenaean Greeks
alongside western Anatolian groups like the Luwians.
Reliefs clearly portray them traveling with oxcarts, women, and children,
signaling that they were not merely raiders,
but desperate refugees fleeing catastrophe elsewhere.
A remarkable scientific breakthrough sheds light here:
a landmark 2019 study published in Nature Human Behaviour
analyzed ancient DNA extracted from early Philistine tombs at Ashkelon, Israel.
The genomic results revealed distinct southern European ancestry
in the founding individuals,
providing direct biological proof of migration originating from the Aegean.
Yet the Sea Peoples cannot explain the entire collapse.
Scholars point out they cannot account for the destruction of mainland Greece,
and early Greeks were likely among the sea migrants themselves.
Most researchers now view them as a symptom of a broader crisis rather than its sole cause.
What, then, was the root cause?
Modern science paints a multi-layered, systemic picture.
Sediment cores extracted from the Aegean Sea
and the Sea of Galilee reveal this was the most arid climatic period in the entire Bronze Age,
characterized by prolonged spikes in temperature and plunging rainfall.
Egypt and Babylon weathered the drought thanks to the perennial Nile and Tigris,
whereas rain-fed agricultural zones suffered devastating crop failures.
Compounding this, archaeological data reveals evidence of sequential earthquake swarms across the region.
Here historians identify a crucial systemic vulnerability:
their very connectivity was their fatal flaw.
The Bronze Age economy hinged on bronze, requiring tin and copper shipped across perilous distances.
When one critical link severed, the entire supply chain fractured.
A system overly complex and hyper-interconnected,
struck simultaneously by environmental and military shocks,
can collapse like a row of falling dominoes.
This phenomenon is known as 'systemic collapse'—
not attributable to any single monocausal event
such as a lone invasion or an isolated earthquake.
It was the lethal resonance of megadrought, famine,
earthquakes, mass migration, warfare, and fractured trade arteries.
And here lies the true historical void:
in the wake of the collapse, written records vanished across multiple civilizations,
archives were extinguished,
and we must rely entirely on material evidence unearthed by archaeology—
ash layers, altered ceramic typologies, and abandoned palaces—
to piece together what truly occurred.
Many Sea Peoples groups, outside the Philistines, simply melted into post-collapse history without leaving a trace.
On historical objectivity:
revisionist scholars like David Rohl have proposed alternative chronologies,
arguing the collapse did not unfold in the orthodox sequence.
However, this remains a fringe perspective,
and the scientific consensus firmly upholds the collapse around 1200 BC.
part3: Around the year 2500 BC,
contemporary with the pyramid builders of Egypt
and the great city-states of Sumer in Mesopotamia,
a third monumental civilization flourished in South Asia,
occupying parts of modern Pakistan and northwest India:
the Indus Valley Civilization,
also known as the Harappan Civilization.
Geographically, it was the most expansive of all three Bronze Age giants,
covering over one million square kilometers—
an area larger than the ancient Near Eastern empires combined.
At its zenith, the civilization encompassed over a thousand settlements,
anchored by great planned cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro,
housing populations estimated between one and five million people.
What makes the Indus Valley extraordinary is its urban sophistication:
cities laid out on precise grid systems with standardized baked brick architecture,
covered drainage networks carrying household waste out of the city,
and private bathrooms in residential homes—
innovations that would not reappear elsewhere
for more than a thousand years.
Yet a profound anomaly baffles archaeologists:
there are no visible monumental palaces for monarchs,
no triumphal victory monuments, and no colossal royal tombs like those in Egypt.
Archaeologists continue to debate the governance structure of this society.
A famous landmark is the 'Great Bath' at Mohenjo-daro,
suggesting a communal ritual significance,
yet its precise social function remains an open question.
And then, there is the writing.
The Indus people left over four thousand inscribed seals and artifacts,
comprising between four hundred and six hundred distinct signs.
They were engraved on small steatite stamp seals, terracotta tablets, and pottery.
This represents the earliest writing system of the Indian subcontinent.
And to this day, after over a century of scholarship, no one has deciphered it.
Why has decipherment proven so extraordinarily difficult?
Linguists identify several compounding obstacles.
First, the texts are exceedingly brief.
The average inscription length is a mere five symbols.
The longest text ever recovered contains only 34 signs.
Compared to the Rosetta Stone,
which unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs by providing identical text in three parallel scripts,
we possess nothing of the kind.
Second, there are no bilingual inscriptions.
There is no 'Indus Rosetta Stone'—
no text pairing the Indus script alongside a known language for comparative analysis.
Third, we do not know what spoken language family it recorded.
Eminent scholars, like Professor Asko Parpola of the University of Helsinki,
who has studied the script since 1968,
hypothesize that it encodes an ancestral Dravidian language.
However, other scholars harbor an even more fundamental skepticism:
questioning whether the signs represent a true phonological writing system at all,
or merely a non-linguistic sign system of heraldic crests and trade symbols,
akin to emblems or trademarks.
Fourth, the scribal tradition severed completely when the civilization declined.
Brahmi, the next major historical script to appear in India centuries later,
exhibits dramatic evolutionary divergence, providing no discernible bridge.
Researchers have attempted myriad decipherment methodologies.
One team employed World War II cryptanalysis algorithms, treating symbols as ciphers.
They made minor statistical strides, but stalled before the script's intricate complexity.
Recently, initiatives have digitized thousands of inscribed sherds across archaeological sites
to cross-reference Indus sign sequences against corpus databases.
The state government of Tamil Nadu in India even announced
a one-million-dollar bounty for anyone,
scholar or amateur alike, who successfully deciphers it.
Yet so far, the code remains unbroken.
What precipitated the decline of this magnificent culture?
Around 1900 BC, the mature Harappan phase began to unravel.
Climatological research indicates this resulted from regional climate shifts,
environmental degradation, and particularly the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra river system,
which had sustained numerous agricultural settlements.
Certain settlements, like Chanhu-daro, were abandoned as the Indus River avulsed and altered course.
Crucially, this was not an abrupt apocalypse as popularly imagined.
Between roughly 1900 and 1300 BC, an orderly de-urbanization unfolded:
major cities were gradually evacuated,
and populations dispersed into smaller rural agricultural communities.
The Indus people did not vanish into thin air; they decentralized.
Yet what we lost,
and may lose forever without a bilingual breakthrough, is their authentic voice.
We know they traded, we know they built,
we know they engraved thousands of seals depicting majestic beasts
and mysterious glyphs.
Yet we do not know what they called themselves,
what mythology they shared,
or what thoughts crossed their minds as they walked away from their cities.
part4: We turn now to another continent,
and a vastly later historical epoch,
demonstrating that historical voids are not confined to the distant ancient world.
Around the year 1050 AD,
in what is today the state of Illinois in the United States,
the Mississippian culture erected a monumental urban center
that we know today as Cahokia.
The name 'Cahokia' was not what its builders called it;
it was named after an indigenous tribe inhabiting the region centuries later.
At its zenith, Cahokia stood as the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico.
At its urban core lay a colossal Grand Plaza spanning approximately fifty acres,
where thousands of residents gathered for religious festivals,
athletic games, and major public proclamations,
encircled by over a hundred monumental earthen platform mounds.
Cahokia operated an expansive continental trade network,
importing copper from the Great Lakes and marine shells from the Gulf of Mexico.
This thoroughly shatters the outdated myth of simple 'primitive hunter-gatherers'
frequently imagined regarding pre-Columbian North America.
This was an advanced agrarian society with complex urban planning,
intricate cosmological rituals,
and monumental earthen engineering.
Yet by roughly 1400 AD, this thriving metropolis was completely abandoned.
And here lies the profound historical void: the Mississippians possessed no written script known to us.
There are no written chronicles, no inscriptions explaining their departure.
We have not a single text articulating why they walked away.
Cahokia left behind only towering earthen mounds, potsherds, post-holes, and unanswered questions.
Archaeologists have proposed multiple working hypotheses:
severe climate anomalies and disastrous river floods,
environmental overexploitation,
particularly catastrophic deforestation for palisades, social factionalism,
and a crisis of faith in ruling religious elites.
Other theories suggest nutritional stress
and disease epidemics may have accelerated the decline.
Yet it must be emphasized: these remain hypotheses,
without definitive scholarly consensus regarding the precise trigger.
Perhaps the most striking lesson of Cahokia is a stark contrast:
a metropolis rivaling contemporary European capitals in size,
yet virtually absent from history textbooks across the modern world.
It reminds us that recorded history depends profoundly on who
leaves behind a written script, not merely on who built extraordinary monuments.
part5: And now, we return home.
If you live in Vietnam,
there is a profound historical void resting right beneath your feet,
in the fertile lands known today as An Giang Province,
within the Mekong Delta.
From roughly the first to the seventh century AD,
this region was the thriving epicenter of an ancient realm
that Chinese dynastic chronicles recorded as Funan.
Funan is widely regarded as the earliest major historical kingdom in Southeast Asia.
Its origins, according to a foundation legend preserved in Chinese court archives,
trace back to a foreign traveler named Huntian who established the dynasty around the first century.
Its primary port metropolis,
known today through the archaeological site of Óc Eo,
was a dazzling cosmopolitan trade emporium.
Interconnected by an elaborate network of engineered canals,
Óc Eo linked directly to maritime ports
and the inland political center of Angkor Borei,
suggesting these sister sites jointly formed the core axis of Funan.
And the material culture unearthed here is utterly breathtaking.
At Óc Eo, archaeologists discovered trade artifacts from Rome,
Persia, India, and Hellenistic Greece,
including silver Roman imperial coins bearing portraits of Roman emperors.
Some classical scholars hypothesize that Óc Eo may correspond to the great maritime port
Greek and Roman geographers designated as 'Cattigara'.
This proves that this southern Vietnamese delta region was once
a vital crossroad on the global maritime silk road linking the Mediterranean to Imperial China.
Inscriptional evidence reveals Funan elites utilized Sanskrit,
a testament to early Indian cultural and religious influence.
Furthermore, contemporary archaeological research demonstrates that Óc Eo culture had deep indigenous roots,
anchored by a population speaking Malayo-Polynesian languages,
far from being a passive 'Indian colony' as colonial historiography once assumed.
So why is this considered a major historical void?
Because for centuries following the decline of
Funan around the sixth to seventh centuries,
the ruins of Óc Eo lay buried, forgotten by the outside world.
Only fragmented mentions in imperial Chinese court records
attested that this great maritime kingdom had ever existed.
Until 1942, when French archaeologists led by Louis Malleret
rediscovered the lost site using aerial reconnaissance photographs,
which revealed the telltale grid traces of ancient canals etched into the earth below.
Excavations officially commenced on February 10, 1942.
And thanks to Malleret's pioneering work, our understanding of Funan took tangible form.
Following 1975, archaeological research on Funan in Vietnam underwent a dynamic revival,
uncovering substantial new material evidence
that allowed researchers to reconstruct the daily lives of Funan's ancient inhabitants.
Between 2017 and 2020,
a major multi-disciplinary excavation campaign was launched across the Óc Eo Ba Thê complex
and the adjacent Nền Chùa sanctuary.
The Óc Eo Ba Thê complex is recognized as the political
and economic heart of Óc Eo culture, spanning over 450 hectares.
Yet despite over seventy-five years of research since
its initial discovery, Óc Eo still guards many unresolved enigmas.
The kingdom fragmented around the seventh century,
yet archaeological evidence reveals that many of its cultural traditions
were preserved and advanced by subsequent southern communities.
Beside Funan, another poignant historical chasm exists in our land: the kingdom of Champa.
Champa endured for over a millennium,
from roughly 500 to 1700 AD,
along the central and southern coastal ribbons of modern Vietnam.
It was a brilliant maritime civilization whose red-brick temple towers still grace the landscape today.
Champa lost its sovereign independence to Đại Việt, marked by the pivotal campaign of 1471.
Yet there is a deeply reflective detail: Champa scribes wrote predominantly on treated palm leaves,
and these perishable manuscripts could not withstand the humid tropical climate of coastal Vietnam.
Today, our primary epigraphic records of Champa derive almost entirely from stone stelae inscriptions,
and many of these stone monuments remain exposed and weathering.
Vast treasures of classical Cham sacred art were lost to time,
to grave looting, and to ancient military conquests.
We know this directly through the surviving inscriptions,
where Cham kings cataloged lavish golden treasures dedicated to temples—
regalia that exists today only in words.
This compels us to reconsider how we conceptualize history.
Champa was long viewed as a centralized monarchy,
yet modern scholarship increasingly suggests
it operated as a decentralized confederation of autonomous river-valley polities,
alternating between federation and regional division throughout its history.
The Cham people remain a vibrant, living indigenous community in Vietnam today.
Understanding Champa and Funan challenges the notion
that Vietnamese history is a single, monolithic, linear story.
part6: Now let us step back and examine all four historical narratives simultaneously.
Are they merely four random, unrelated historical episodes?
Or is there a deeper universal pattern at play?
Upon close analysis, we can identify at least three core mechanisms that create historical voids.
The first mechanism: literacy vanishes when the scribal elite collapses.
During the Bronze Age Collapse, palace scribal writing dissolved with the palaces themselves.
When centralized political institutions fractured,
the trained scribal class, administrative archives,
and the economic incentive to maintain written records evaporated.
A historical chasm frequently begins at the exact moment
the individuals capable of recording events are swept up in the catastrophe.
The second mechanism: the script survives, but the cipher to read it is lost.
This is the reality of the Indus Valley Civilization.
We possess thousands of inscriptions, but lack the linguistic bridge to translate them.
Sometimes a void is not a lack of physical data,
but the absence of a Rosetta Stone connecting their dead language to ours.
The third mechanism: recording media were inherently perishable,
or a society recorded its memory in forms modern scholars fail to recognize.
Cahokia left behind no written texts known to us.
The Cham wrote on organic palm leaves that decayed in the humid tropical climate.
This exemplifies what historians term 'survival bias':
we possess intimate knowledge of cultures that inscribed durable fired clay,
granite, or papyri preserved in arid desert climates,
yet understand far less about civilizations that recorded their world on perishable media.
And there is an even deeper philosophical truth underlying all three mechanisms:
a chasm in our historical record does not indicate a void in human lived experience.
It merely reflects a void in surviving physical evidence.
The Indus people lived, loved, traded,
and conducted spirited debates that we can no longer hear.
The citizens of Cahokia celebrated rituals and shared stories that no living memory retains.
The merchants of Funan sailed to India,
exchanged goods with imperial Rome,
and today we know their sovereign name primarily through the chronicles of a neighbor.
The fact that we do not know what transpired does not mean nothing happened.
part7: The history taught in schoolrooms often resembles a straight, paved highway.
Yet when you step off the main thoroughfare,
you realize it is far more like an active archaeological excavation:
unmatched ceramic sherds, and ancient inscriptions waiting to be read.
Today, an archaeologist is patiently brushing the delta soil from a potsherd in An Giang.
A linguist is cross-referencing sign sequences on an Indus seal
with inscribed pottery discovered thousands of miles away.
A paleogeneticist is extracting ancient DNA from a three-thousand-year-old tomb,
tracing the footsteps of ancestors who melted into the mists of history without leaving their names.
These historical silences are not permanent, immutable voids.
They are unwritten chapters of our human story, and each year, line by patient line, we are filling them in.
